questions.subtopic: 4C2 Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB and Basel. Sharing with a foreign regulator
questions.question: A foreign auditor oversight authority asks the PCAOB for confidential inspection findings on a registered firm it also regulates. Under Section 105(b)(5)(C), added by Dodd-Frank, when may the Board share them?

options.A: At its discretion, if necessary and with the foreign body's assurances
options.B: On request, because Dodd-Frank obliges it to share with foreign bodies
options.C: After SEC approval, because the Board cannot share on its own
options.D: Whenever the foreign body gives confidentiality assurances, as of right

questions.key_concept: Since Dodd-Frank Section 981, the PCAOB may share confidential information with foreign auditor regulators, at its discretion and on set conditions.
questions.pre_read: Read whether the provision creates a power or a duty, and list every condition it sets.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 981 added Section 105(b)(5)(C): the Board may, at its discretion, give confidential information to a foreign auditor oversight authority if it finds sharing necessary for the Act's purposes or investor protection, the foreign body gives confidentiality assurances and describes its information systems and relevant laws, and the Board finds sharing appropriate. The information stays confidential and privileged in the Board's hands.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Dodd-Frank opened the door to sharing. But the statute says 'may, at the discretion of the Board'; it creates no duty to share.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC oversees the Board. But Section 105(b)(5)(C) leaves sharing to the Board's discretion and sets no SEC approval step.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: assurances are one condition. The Board must also find sharing necessary and appropriate, and receive descriptions of the body's systems and laws.

tips: Eliminate: B turns a discretionary power into a duty, and C adds an SEC approval step the provision does not set.
Final two: A beats D because sharing stays at the Board's discretion and needs its own findings, not only the foreign body's assurances.
Exam cue: 'may, at the discretion of' signals a power with conditions, not a duty; check every condition.

questions.subtopic: 4C3 The Sarbanes-Oxley amendments. Indemnity for recovered pay
questions.question: A listed issuer must recover $200,000 of erroneously awarded incentive pay from its former COO under its Rule 10D-1 policy, and the board proposes to indemnify the COO for that loss. The proposal:

options.A: is allowed if the independent directors approve it
options.B: is allowed because the COO has already left the issuer
options.C: is barred unless the indemnity is disclosed in the proxy
options.D: is barred, as the rule forbids indemnity against recovery

questions.key_concept: Rule 10D-1 forbids an issuer from indemnifying current or former executive officers against recovery of erroneously awarded pay.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the rule leaves any route for the issuer to make the executive whole.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10D-1(b)(1)(v) prohibits the issuer from indemnifying any executive officer or former executive officer against the loss of erroneously awarded compensation. The recovery duty covers former executive officers too, so the COO's departure changes nothing. Independent directors matter only for the narrow impracticability exceptions, such as recovery costs exceeding the amount; they cannot approve an indemnity.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: independent directors decide the impracticability exceptions. But no approval can authorize indemnifying an executive against recovery; the rule bars it outright.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the COO is gone. But Rule 10D-1 recovery reaches former executive officers, and the indemnity bar covers them too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because disclosure often cures conflicts. But the indemnity ban has no disclosure exception.

tips: Eliminate: B forgets that recovery reaches former executive officers, and C invents a disclosure exception to the indemnity ban.
Final two: D beats A because Rule 10D-1 bars that indemnity outright; independent directors decide only the impracticability exceptions.
Exam cue: Rule 10D-1 recovery is no-fault, reaches former officers and cannot be undone by an issuer indemnity.

options.C: No; the rule excludes staff of foreign financial regulators
options.D: No; the program pays U.S. citizens and residents alone

questions.key_concept: Rule 21F-8(c)(2) bars awards to staff of foreign governments and foreign financial regulators; citizenship is not the test.
questions.pre_read: Ask who employed the tipster when they learned the facts, and where the SEC's rule adds to the statute.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 21F-8(c)(2) makes ineligible anyone who is, or was when they got the information, a member, officer or employee of a foreign government or a foreign financial regulatory authority. The statute's own list names no foreign regulator, but the SEC's rule extends the bar to them. Nationality is not the test; the examiner's employer is.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the statute's list in 78u-6(c)(2)(A) names no foreign regulator. But Rule 21F-8(c)(2) adds foreign governments and foreign financial regulators, so the examiner is excluded.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because some rules credit internal reports. But reporting to their own regulator cannot cure the examiner's exclusion under Rule 21F-8(c)(2).
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the program is a U.S. one. But a whistleblower is any individual who reports to the SEC; the exclusion here turns on the examiner's employer.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a report to the examiner's own regulator cure an exclusion, and D adds a citizenship test the law does not set.
Final two: C beats A because Rule 21F-8(c)(2) extends the statute's exclusion of regulators' staff to foreign governments and foreign regulators.
Exam cue: for award eligibility, check who employed the tipster when they learned the facts, not where they live.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 The Securities Act and the Exchange Act. What registration does not mean
questions.question: A company's registration statement for its first share offering has become effective, and its investor relations lead wants to tell buyers the SEC has vouched for the shares. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The SEC has confirmed that the disclosures are accurate and complete
options.B: The SEC requires accurate disclosure, but it does not guarantee it
options.C: The SEC has judged the shares a sound investment for buyers
options.D: Effectiveness shields the company from later claims of false disclosure

questions.key_concept: The Securities Act relies on disclosure: the SEC requires accurate information but does not guarantee it or judge an offering's merits.
questions.pre_read: Ask what registration gives investors, and who is left to judge the investment.
questions.correct_explanation: The SEC calls the Securities Act the 'truth in securities' law: registration gives investors the facts so that they, not the government, judge whether to buy. The SEC requires accurate information but does not guarantee it. Section 23 adds that effectiveness is no finding that the statement is accurate or approval of the shares, and it makes telling buyers otherwise unlawful.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the SEC does require accurate disclosure. But it does not guarantee or confirm accuracy; investors can still recover if disclosure proves inaccurate.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC reviews filings. But the Act relies on disclosure so investors, not the government, judge the merits of buying.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the statement passed SEC review. But buyers keep recovery rights if they prove incomplete or inaccurate disclosure.

tips: Eliminate: C has the SEC judge investment merit, which the disclosure system leaves to investors, and D treats effectiveness as a shield against disclosure claims.
Final two: B beats A because the SEC requires accurate disclosure but does not guarantee it; effectiveness is not a confirmation of accuracy.
Exam cue: the 1933 Act is about disclosure, not merit; the SEC never vouches for an offering.
